Oncology FAQs
What are VSRC Oncology’s service hours and appointment times?
VSRC Oncology sees appointments and treats patients Monday through Friday.
While drop-off chemo appointments are preferred for existing patients, accommodations can be made on a case-by-case basis if specific appointment times during the day are desired.
New consults, recheck visits, and same-day appointments are seen throughout the day as scheduled appointments, however we generally do not accommodate in-hospital appointments – particularly new consultations – after 4p. This allows us to provide the highest level of medical care, safely, for our patients, and permits adequate time to discuss and develop treatment plans.
Concierge (in-home) visits are available on a case-by-case basis and may be arranged outside of normal service hours where possible, however injectable chemotherapy, electrochemotherapy, and immunotherapy must be administered in-hospital. Please contact us directly for more information.
For patients undergoing scheduled procedures requiring sedation or anesthesia (for example electrochemotherapy, CT scan), our service coordinator will contact you to discuss timing and preparation for your pet’s visit.
We are an outpatient clinic and do not provide overnight care or boarding. Patient discharge is no later than 5:45p (15 minutes before the close of the practice) during hospital hours.
What should I expect at my first Oncology appointment?
The main goal of the initial Oncology consultation is to exchange all of the information necessary to make the best decisions for your companion. You will receive a thorough explanation of your pet’s condition, testing recommendations, and a treatment plan. Each patient is unique, and the VSRC Oncology team will work closely with you to develop a bespoke treatment plan for your pet’s needs.
Bloodwork, imaging tests, and potentially starting cancer treatment may all be possible during the first visit. Costs of all testing and treatment will be provided at the time of your visit.
Your first consultation will likely last about one hour. It is best to block off at least 90 minutes of time for your appointment from start to finish. If further diagnostics are performed at the initial appointment, this will take additional time.
What should I bring to my appointment?
It is most important that you bring your companion! By meeting face-to-face, we can begin to build a relationship with your pet and personally assess their physical condition. The physical examination performed at an initial visit provides invaluable information to your oncologist, which may factor into treatment recommendations or clinical decision-making going forward.
It is a good idea when possible to bring notes summarizing any behavioral or physical changes you may notice at home, as well as specific questions that you may have for your oncologist. Even subtle changes in routine or behavior can provide us with very important information.
While we request medical records in advance from your veterinarian, please bring an extra copy of your pet’s records to your initial consultation, particularly if new test results are available since your last visit with your primary veterinarian.
Will my primary veterinarian be involved in my pet’s care and treatment plan?
Absolutely! It takes a village, and we firmly believe the most effective cancer treatment involves collaboration amongst your pet’s entire medical team, including your primary veterinarian. After your appointment, your oncologist will send your primary veterinarian a detailed report and begin establishing a partnered plan for treating your pet.
Will other veterinary specialists be involved in my pet’s care?
Because all patients are unique, sometimes other veterinary specialists (such as surgeons, cardiologists, neurologists, radiologists, or internists) may be consulted before, during, or after your pet’s treatment. If the oncologist believes your companion could benefit from the expertise of additional specialists, we may discuss this with you during your appointment.
How much does cancer treatment cost?
Veterinary oncologists understand that finances are an important part of decision-making with regard to your pet’s cancer care. Cost is highly variable depending upon the cancer being treated, any co-existent medical concerns your pet may have, and the exact treatments involved.
You will be provided with an itemized list of price estimates for the diagnostic and treatment options discussed, at the time of or shortly after your visit. All treatments are pay-as-you-go, and payment is made at the time services are rendered.
Pet insurance is often very helpful in covering a portion of a pet’s cancer-related costs, including diagnostic tests and treatment. We will work with your pet’s insurance company to facilitate timely reimbursement post-visit.
If your pet is not insured, while we do not offer payment plans as such, services such as Care Credit or Scratch Pay may help with staging the cost of treatment. Please contact us directly for more information.
What is electrochemotherapy?
Electrochemotherapy is a versatile treatment with an excellent safety profile that can be administered as a single therapy, or in conjunction with chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and radiation therapy.
Electrochemotherapy utilizes reversible electroporation via gentle electrical pulses applied directly to the tumor tissue or scar by means of specialized needle electrodes that allow the treatment of different anatomical sites (both superficial and deep-seated).
Chemotherapy is administered intravenously during this procedure.
Electrochemotherapy is a non-thermal method, which means that the procedure does not raise the temperature of the electroporated tissue. This preserves the health of tissue adjacent to the site being treated and significantly reduces the risk of more severe side effects.
Electrochemotherapy is administered under heavy sedation or general anesthesia. This is done to ensure efficient and safe treatment by minimizing patient movement and discomfort.
There is no required ‘down time’ after an electrochemotherapy treatment, per se, however a patient may be slightly groggy the day of treatment as they recover from the sedation or anesthetic drugs used.
With the treatment of microscopic disease, treatments are typically administered every 3-4 weeks, for a total of 1-3 treatments. Minor redness or dryness, hair loss, and hyperpigmentation (darkening) of the treated tissue may occur post-treatment.
Regression of macroscopic tumors may take several weeks or longer to occur post-treatment, however the average time to maximum effect is 6-8 weeks.
Electrochemotherapy
may be used to treat a variety of different tumor types including oral, perianal, and skin tumors, as well as microscopic residual disease (tumor ‘bed’/surgical scar).
How is chemotherapy administered?
Chemotherapy comes in oral (taken by mouth) and injectable forms (given with a needle, either through a vein/intravenously, under the skin/subcutaneously, or within the muscle; directly into a tumor; or into a body cavity or space).
How is immunotherapy administered?
The exact method depends on the immunotherapy! Generally speaking however, immunotherapies are injected into the body.
What is a small molecule inhibitor (SMI) and when might one be prescribed for my pet?
SMIs are usually given orally. These medications interfere with various signaling processes that are involved in promoting tumor growth and spread.
SMIs may be prescribed as part of a multi-drug treatment protocol or may be prescribed alone for the treatment of various cancers. At VSRC Oncology, we prefer to pair mutation analysis on tumor tissue samples with SMI therapy whenever possible. Tumor mutation analysis better informs SMI treatment and allows us to avail our patients of all possible options.
Can I be present or hold my pet while they are receiving chemotherapy?
We do not permit anyone to accompany their pet within the Oncology suite, for the following reasons:
Chemotherapy drugs present direct exposure risks to humans. While we take every precaution to minimize these risks for our team, we do accept some risk for ourselves, given the nature of what we do. We do not, however, accept transferring this exposure risk to our clients.
The logistics of giving chemotherapy to animals differs from that of people – our patients do not fully understand what we are doing, and they may try to get up and move around during chemo administration. Our staff is highly trained in gentle but expert restraint for chemotherapy to ensure efficient and safe drug delivery. Any significant movement of the patient during chemotherapy administration risks extravasation (getting chemo drug outside the vein), which can lead to a degree of tissue irritation or damage that in some cases may be severe. While we do everything we can to minimize the risk of extravasation and thankfully this is a rare complication, having a pet’s human present in the room adds an extra variable that may increase this risk.
We understand the desire to be present and see the process, however in reality, we find that animals are often much calmer without their humans around during their treatments. Rest assured that our paramount concern is patient comfort and safety – if we feel that your pet is not tolerating chemo administration well (overly anxious, wiggly, etc), we will be fully transparent with you and offer suggestions to maximize their comfort during the process.
How long does chemotherapy take to give? How long will my chemo appointments be?
It varies. Oral drugs are typically given at the time of the visit with a small amount of food, or sent home with very specific instructions as to how and when to give these medications.
Injectable chemotherapy medications are administered within VSRC’s Oncology suite. Many injectable chemo drugs are ‘quick’ (bolus) injections, while others require an infusion over time, or may require sedation, which can extend treatment times (for example, with intracavitary administration).
Chemo visits last on average between 1-3 hours, but the time needed is highly variable based on a number of factors. Drop-off chemo appointments are preferred for this reason.
How does a chemo drop-off appointment work?
Chemotherapy drop-off patients should plan to arrive at VSRC between 8-9a. A physical examination and in-house bloodwork are performed at each visit prior to chemo administration.
Patient discharge may happen throughout the day when treatments are completed, however we can hold pets for the day if needed. VSRC closes promptly at 6p; all patients must be discharged no later than 15 minutes prior to close.
If special accommodation is needed, occasional exceptions may be made for a mid-day drop-off time on a case-by-case basis.
What are the side effects of chemotherapy and how do I manage them?
No treatment is completely benign. While we adjust our dosages to reflect the patients we are treating and aim to minimize, if not eliminate, any side effects of therapy, they can and do happen in a subset of patients.
General side effects of chemotherapy may include stomach upset, lethargy, and bone marrow suppression (typically a decrease in the white blood cell and/or platelet counts, sometimes mild anemia); these are typically mild to moderate and self-limiting, or treatable with supportive medications.
A few chemotherapy drugs have the potential for rare but unique side effects, which will be discussed in detail at your visit if your pet is receiving one of these drugs.
Most of our patients exhibit very good tolerance of chemotherapy, with minimal if any side effects from treatment. We can typically avoid or successfully treat mild to moderate side effects with supportive medications given at home. Side effects requiring hospitalization can occur, though are rare.
Side effects will be discussed in detail as your pet’s treatment progresses so that you are informed of the potential risks versus benefits of therapy as we go along. Treatment plans are dynamic and tailored to each patient.  It is important to remember that we can change or stop treatment at any time, for any reason, and particularly if you are not comfortable with the course of therapy, or if we feel your pet is not responding well to treatment or is having unanticipated side effects.
OK, but really, is my pet just going to be super sick from treatment? What if they’re afraid of coming to the vet regularly? I don’t want them to be miserable the whole time.
Neither do we! The process of treatment and any side effects from chemotherapy do not typically prevent our patients from enjoying a full, active lifestyle (or remaining a happy couch potato, if that’s their thing) – this is the whole point of treatment! Chemotherapy patients can and do hike, fly, frolic in the park, play, attend family gatherings and social events, and in general live their best dog and cat lives while receiving treatment.
Quality of life considerations on chemo are paramount. We will provide thorough information at the time of your visit regarding how to recognize and monitor your pet’s side effects at home, dispense medications to prevent or treat any adverse effects, and provide guidance regarding when a visit to the veterinarian is required to address side effects.
We have a consistent, compassionate Oncology team to receive your pet and make their experience as gentle and kind as possible. The majority of our patients get well used to the routine of coming for regular visits and treatments, and adapt accordingly. We are highly sensitive to quality of life concerns for all of our patients, and provide a quiet, calm space for our patients to minimize stress.
What do I have to know about exposure risk to myself and my family for my pet who is receiving chemotherapy?
Exposure risk for family members is generally exceptionally low, and usually not of significant concern on a day-to-day basis, though we will address this on an individual basis during your pet’s treatment.
Anything else?
Constructive communication is a vital part of the treatment process. Oncology treatment is a team effort, involving communication between the Oncology team, your primary veterinarian, other veterinarians and care providers who may be involved in your pet’s case, and yourself.  If something is not working for you or your pet, or if you have questions or concerns at any time, please let us know directly. We cannot help if we are not aware!
There is a wealth of misinformation and false information out in the world and online regarding oncologic treatments and outcomes in veterinary patients. It is our job as veterinary oncologists to use our training and clinical experience to provide clear, up-to-date information, so that you can make informed decisions regarding treatment that we feel is in the best interests of your pet.  We appreciate and welcome people’s desire to educate themselves on their pet’s cancer and treatment options – and we love having deep discussions about all of it – however you can be confident that we are presenting you with up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations that are informed and honed by many years of clinical experience.
The ideal medical recommendation(s) will be presented at each visit; we may provide additional options that are reasonable to consider, and the outcomes one might expect with each of these options in turn.
If you are not satisfied with an initial opinion, feel that you have unanswered questions, or have concerns about your pet, direct communication is vital. Please let us know what’s going on via email
oncology@vsrcmanhattan.com
or phone
(646) 632-2538
.
Sometimes a second opinion can be helpful to solidify options in one’s mind and help arrive at a decision on next steps. If a second opinion or outside referral (for example, for radiation therapy) is desired or necessary, we will facilitate medical records transfer to another hospital upon request.
Our Oncology email address is checked regularly, however urgent matters should
not
be communicated via email. You should expect up to 24-48 hours for a response to email given the volume of messages we receive.
If your pet is experiencing an emergency or appears to be in crisis, please bring them immediately to the closest Emergency Service. We are not a walk-in clinic, and VSRC is not equipped to treat animals requiring urgent care or emergency/critical intervention and management.
And finally – please be kind. We recognize that New Yorkers have busy lives with packed schedules and places to be, and we respect our client’s time. Know that our team deeply cares about your and your pet’s experience – always! – but veterinary medicine can be an unpredictable beast (pun intended). We endeavor to get your pet evaluated, treated, and home to you as soon as possible, however there may be unanticipated delays in a patient’s treatment on any given day due to any number of contributing factors.  We do our level best to provide the best experience we can. Please know that if there is a delay, or if things don’t go exactly as prefaced or planned with your pet’s visit, it is for a good medical reason.
